newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Croatia, Serbia "good neighbours" says minister.
newsitem.headline: Croatia, Serbia "good neighbours" says minister.

text.p: The Yugoslav and Croatian foreign ministers pushed ahead with normalising relations between their countries on Wednesday and said talks in the Serbian capital had added impetus to the process.

"We had a constructive meeting and agreed on a number of issues. They represent a considerable speeding up of overall Yugoslav-Croatian relations which are the backbone of relations in the Balkans and in our region in general," Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic said.
He told reporters after meeting Croatia's Mate Granic they had reached agreement on nearly all of 18 issues discussed.
"We will endeavour in the next few weeks to wind up the whole business and make it ready to be signed. We have given all these talks a political impetus."

It was the third time the two ministers have met since signing accords for full diplomatic relations on August 23 last year, after a surprise summit between Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
The accords marked the end of a conflict that began after Croatia's independence from federal Yugoslavia, but left a host of bilateral problems to be solved in future talks.
"The very fact that Mr Granic is here today with us...shows that our overall relations are on an upward slope, that they are good-neighbourly," Milutinovic said.
Croatia said in December the normalisation of its relations with Yugoslavia, from which it seceded in 1991, was too slow.

Granic said he and Milutinovic talked about issues including citizenship, frontier trade and traffic, border crossings, cooperation between Interior Ministries and the rights of Croats in Yugoslavia and of Serbs in Croatia.
They are expected to sign agreements in two or three months on rail, road and air traffic, succession talks, missing persons and refugees and property issues.

Granic said he and Milutinovic agreed that the process of reintegrating the region of Eastern Slavonia in Croatian territory was making good progress. Around 120,000 Serbs live in the last Serb-held enclave in Croatia which is due to revert to Croatian rule after local elections in April.
"With respect to (the Serbs') human and minority rights, they are fully equal citizens of the Republic of Croatia," Granic said.
The Croatian government, in a Letter of Intent to the UN Security Council, pledged a host of Serb rights to encourage those living in the region not to flee.
Serbs were promised posts in ministries, the Office of Refugees and the enclave's two counties as well as proportional representation in the region's police force and judiciary.
Granic said the letter and the Croatian constitution and law were a guarantee of protection of their rights.
